features.name: distinct_factual_premises_challenged_count
features.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments): number of distinct factual premises in the OP's title/argument that are challenged by at least one comment
features.spec: Read title, argument (OP post body, current text incl. marked edits) and OC_comments (JSON list of comments by other users; order carries no meaning) jointly. Count the distinct factual (empirical/descriptive, not purely evaluative, moral or logical-structure) premises stated or clearly relied on in the OP's title/argument that at least one comment explicitly challenges, disputes, or presents evidence against. Deduplicate semantically: the same premise challenged by several comments counts once; different premises count separately. Do not count challenges to values, definitions-as-preference, or merely adding new considerations; do not count premises only mentioned by comments and not in the OP text. Output a non-negative integer: 0 = no comment challenges any OP factual premise. If OC_comments is a valid empty list return 0. If title/argument or OC_comments is missing or malformed return null. Do not use the conversation or any outcome.

features.name: counterargument_cognitive_complexity
features.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments, by users other than OP): overall cognitive complexity of the counterarguments, scored 0-10 by anchored rubric
features.spec: Read the OC_comments JSON list (counter-argument comments by users other than the OP; list order carries no rank or chronology). Judge the cognitive complexity of the counterarguments taken together, using only the comment text (ignore quoted text from others unless adopted by the commenter). Cognitive complexity = differentiation (distinguishing multiple dimensions, perspectives, conditions or cases) plus integration (connecting/weighing them into a nuanced, qualified, reasoned whole), as opposed to simplistic, single-dimension, assertion-only reasoning. Return one number 0-10: 0 = no argumentative content; 2 = bare assertion or single simple point with no reasoning; 4 = one reasoned point with limited elaboration; 6 = several distinct reasons or some acknowledgment of qualifications/alternative views; 8 = multiple dimensions explicitly differentiated with conditions/trade-offs and partly integrated; 10 = highly differentiated and fully integrated, nuanced, multi-perspective reasoning. This is an operational score, not a validated instrument. Do not use length alone. Return null if OC_comments is missing, malformed, or an empty list.

Exclude quoted text from others, reported opponents' positions, moderator/bot notices, and hypothetical or generic statements about people in general, unless explicitly adopted as the OP's own experience. Mere opinions or anger without self-disclosed vulnerability do not count. Return 0 if the text is present and contains no such disclosure. Return null if argument is missing or malformed. Use no other columns.

features.name: any_comment_well_reasoned_counterargument
features.definition: Other users' comments: any comment presents a well-reasoned counterargument to the OP's view (title/argument)
features.spec: Read title, argument (OP view) and OC_comments (JSON list of comments by other users; order is not rank or chronology) jointly. Return 1 if at least one comment directly challenges the OP's stated view with a well-reasoned counterargument: clear, relevant, logically coherent reasoning or evidence that bears on the OP's actual claim, not mere assertion, insult, joke, off-topic remark or pure agreement. Return 0 if the list is valid but empty or no comment qualifies. Return null if OC_comments is missing/malformed or the OP view cannot be determined (title and argument both missing). Do not use any outcome or other columns.

features.name: op_logical_concession_count
features.definition: OP's own replies in the discussion: count of distinct logical concession statements (OP grants a counterpoint's logical validity or acknowledges a flaw/limit in own reasoning)
features.spec: Read conversation together with title and argument. Identify the OP's own replies in the conversation (OP is the author of the post; OP turns may lack a speaker tag or be replies to commenters; use title/argument for context; do not attribute commenters' text to the OP). Count distinct statements by the OP that logically concede: acknowledging that a counterpoint is valid/correct, that their reasoning has a flaw, exception or limitation, or that a point undermines part of their view. Exclude mere politeness/thanks, quoted or reported opponent positions not adopted by OP, moderator/bot notices, and unchanged restatements. Output a non-negative integer count (0 = OP replies present but no such concession). If conversation contains no OP replies that can be identified, output 0 when the conversation is validly present with no OP replies; output null if conversation is missing or malformed. Count of statements over the discussion, not normalised by length.

features.name: any_comment_cites_numerical_data
features.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments): any comment contains specific numerical data or statistics supporting its argument
features.spec: Read the OC_comments JSON list (comments by users other than the OP). Return 1 if at least one comment contains specific numerical data or statistics (e.g., concrete figures, percentages, rates, counts, measured quantities, or cited statistical findings) used in its argument. Return 0 if the list is valid and nonempty but no comment has such specifics (general assertions, reasoning, or non-quantitative examples only; incidental numbers like list numbering or generic words such as 'one' do not count). Quoted OP text does not count unless the commenter supplies data. Return null if OC_comments is missing or malformed; a valid empty list returns 0. Do not use the conversation, later replies or any outcome.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument includes explicit comparisons to established scientific or historical norms are associated with lower view change than those without such comparisons.
hypotheses.h0: Mean delta does not differ between discussions with and without argument_compares_to_established_norms.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with argument_compares_to_established_norms=1 have lower delta than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: "Established norms" is interpreted as accepted scientific or historical standards/precedents; boundary is somewhat subjective. Uses current argument text, no initial snapshot.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Arguments expressing explicit fear of social rejection or isolation are associated with lower view-change rates than arguments stating beliefs without emotional self-defense.
hypotheses.h0: Mean delta rate does not differ between posts with op_expresses_fear_of_social_rejection_or_isolation and posts with op_states_belief_without_emotional_self_defense (beta_fear = beta_plain).
hypotheses.h1: Posts with op_expresses_fear_of_social_rejection_or_isolation have a lower view-change rate than posts with op_states_belief_without_emotional_self_defense (beta_fear < beta_plain).
hypotheses.note: The claim is a contrast between two named groups (fear vs plain-belief). In this OLS each coefficient is relative to the residual group (posts with other emotional self-defense but no explicit fear), so neither coefficient alone is the fear-minus-plain difference (beta_fear - beta_plain); that would need a linear-contrast test or subsetting to the two groups, not a single design-matrix term. The two features are mutually exclusive by construction. 'Emotional self-defense' is operationalized per the spec and is not a validated instrument. Hypothesis speaks of 'arguments'; read as the OP's title and post body.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Counter-arguments that cite specific, functioning institutional precedents are associated with a higher probability of view change than those relying on abstract normative principles.
hypotheses.h0: Coefficient of any_comment_cites_functioning_institutional_precedent is zero (given any_comment_relies_on_abstract_normative_principles) for view-change probability.
hypotheses.h1: Coefficient of any_comment_cites_functioning_institutional_precedent is positive relative to any_comment_relies_on_abstract_normative_principles in the model.
hypotheses.note: The claim is a contrast between precedent-citing and abstract-principle comments; the single coefficient tests precedent holding principle fixed, not the difference of the two coefficients. Features are row-level any-comment indicators, not comment-level comparisons; the two can overlap within a row. Linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions featuring longer precomputed log-transformed discussion length are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: log_length_value has no association with the probability that the OP changed their view (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Higher log_length_value is associated with a higher likelihood of OP view change (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: log_length's construction is undocumented (unclear what text it measures); used as supplied. OLS on a binary outcome is a linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains explicit admissions of uncertainty are associated with a higher probability of view change than those asserting absolute certainty.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions whose op_explicit_uncertainty_admission is 1 have the same probability of view change as those where it is 0.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with op_explicit_uncertainty_admission = 1 have a higher probability of view change than those with it = 0.
hypotheses.note: The claim contrasts uncertainty admissions with absolute-certainty assertions. Absolute certainty is not the complement of uncertainty, and the two features can both be 0. The regression compares uncertainty present with absent. It therefore does not isolate the contrast with posts asserting absolute certainty, which are probably rare. op_asserts_absolute_certainty is defined for that comparison but is not in the rhs. Frequency and intensity thresholds are unspecified. It tests association only, not causation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Counter-arguments frequently challenging multiple distinct factual premises within the argument are positively associated with view change.
hypotheses.h0: distinct_factual_premises_challenged_count has no association with view change (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Higher distinct_factual_premises_challenged_count is associated with a higher probability of view change (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis says "frequently" challenging "multiple" premises without a frequency cutoff; none was invented. The count of distinct factual premises challenged across all comments is used as an operational graded measure, not a thresholded "frequent" indicator. Comments are an unordered list, so per-comment frequency/chronology is not captured. Linear model on binary outcome (OLS).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains fewer counter-argument responses are associated with a lower likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: oc_comment_count has no association with the likelihood of the OP changing their view (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Higher oc_comment_count is associated with a higher likelihood of the OP changing their view (coefficient > 0), i.e., fewer comments mean lower likelihood.
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis wording ("original argument contains fewer counter-argument responses") is ambiguous. It is interpreted as the number of counter-argument comments supplied in OC_comments for the row. The supplied list may not be the complete discussion, and its order is not chronological. The test is a linear (OLS) association on the delta outcome and does not control for confounds.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions with at least three distinct counter-arguments in the posted comments are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with has_at_least_three_distinct_counter_arguments = 1 have the same likelihood of OP view change as those with 0.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with has_at_least_three_distinct_counter_arguments = 1 have a higher likelihood of OP view change than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: Distinct counter-arguments are semantically deduplicated and counted within the supplied OC_comments only; the list may be incomplete relative to the full discussion. OLS on binary outcome is a linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original post title uses absolute certainty markers are associated with a lower likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: Title_absolute_certainty_marker has no association with the likelihood of the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.h1: Title_absolute_certainty_marker = 1 is associated with a lower likelihood of the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.note: Binary presence of a marker; "absolute certainty markers" has no fixed lexicon, so the examples are nonexhaustive. Linear probability model on binary delta. Uses the current title text.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where original posts explicitly invite critique or use tentative language are associated with higher view-change rates than those using absolute, definitive declarations.
hypotheses.h0: View-change rates do not differ between posts with op_invites_critique_or_tentative=1 and posts with op_absolute_definitive_declaration=1.
hypotheses.h1: Posts with op_invites_critique_or_tentative=1 have higher view-change rates than posts with op_absolute_definitive_declaration=1.
hypotheses.note: Claim is a contrast between two named groups (tentative/inviting vs absolute). In the OLS with both indicators, beta_A - beta_B is not a single design-matrix coefficient, so no single term represents it; term=null. The two features are not complements and may overlap or both be 0. Uses current post text including edits; no initial snapshot available.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions featuring counter-arguments that explicitly cite specific real-world examples are associated with higher likelihood of original view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_cites_specific_real_world_example has no association with the likelihood of OP view change.
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_cites_specific_real_world_example is positively associated with the likelihood of OP view change.
hypotheses.note: Hypothesis is associative; OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model. Uses current comment text; list order is not chronology. No controls added.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Counterarguments containing measured, logical reasoning are positively associated with the original poster changing their mind compared to those containing emotional aggression in ChangeMyView discussions.
hypotheses.h0: logical_minus_aggressive_any has zero association with the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.h1: logical_minus_aggressive_any is positively associated with the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.note: Hypothesis compares comments with measured logical reasoning vs emotional aggression; operationalized at row level as any-comment indicators and their difference (a row-level proxy, not a comment-level comparison). Rows with both or neither score 0, so the contrast mixes distinct situations and assumes equal and opposite effects. Any vs share/frequency is not specified in the claim. Comment order is unknown; conversation not used (leakage).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly quote and refute specific factual claims in the original post are associated with higher rates of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_quotes_and_refutes_op_factual_claim has no association with delta (view change rate).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_quotes_and_refutes_op_factual_claim is associated with a higher rate of view change (delta).
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis does not specify any vs. all vs. frequency; 'any comment' is used as the operationalization. OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model. Association only, not causal. Factual vs opinion boundary is a semantic judgment.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly validate the original poster's personal dignity or effort before introducing corrective logic are associated with higher view-change rates than purely logical refutations.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with any_comment_validates_op_dignity_or_effort_before_correction and discussions with all_comments_purely_logical_refutation have equal view-change rates.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_validates_op_dignity_or_effort_before_correction have higher view-change rates than discussions with all_comments_purely_logical_refutation.
hypotheses.note: The claim contrasts validate-then-correct with purely logical discussions, i.e. beta_validate - beta_pure, which is not a single coefficient here (each is relative to an omitted residual group). Ordering of validation before correction is judged within a comment only; comment list order is not chronology. The pure feature is null for empty lists.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions featuring counter-arguments that provide concrete real-world examples are associated with a higher likelihood of view change than those relying primarily on abstract reasoning.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_concrete_real_world_example has zero association with the likelihood of view change (delta).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_concrete_real_world_example is positively associated with the likelihood of view change (delta).
hypotheses.note: The "relying primarily on abstract reasoning" comparison group is operationalized as the absence of any concrete example comment; no frequency or dominance cutoff is specified, so "primarily" is not separately measured. Linear probability model via OLS. Comment order and chronology are unknown.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly engage with the specific examples or premises cited in the original argument text are associated with a higher likelihood of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_engages_op_examples_or_premises has no association with view change (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_engages_op_examples_or_premises is associated with higher likelihood of view change (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: Hypothesis says "counter-arguments" without specifying any/all/share; operationalized as any comment. OLS on binary outcome (linear probability). The conversation column is avoided because of outcome leakage.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions featuring counter-arguments that introduce concrete, personal labor-process details are associated with higher view-change rates than those relying solely on abstract normative principles.
hypotheses.h0: Rows with any_comment_concrete_personal_labor_details=1 have the same view-change rate as rows with all_comments_solely_abstract_normative=1.
hypotheses.h1: Rows with any_comment_concrete_personal_labor_details=1 have a higher view-change rate than rows with all_comments_solely_abstract_normative=1.
hypotheses.note: Claim contrasts concrete-labor-detail discussions with solely-abstract-normative ones. In the OLS both indicators share a baseline of neither group, so no single coefficient equals beta_concrete minus beta_abstract; a linear-contrast test would be needed, hence term=null. Frequency/amount of detail is unspecified. conversation not used to avoid leakage. Prompt features are meant to be mutually exclusive by definition.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly quantify systemic material harms to third parties rather than asserting propositional falsity are associated with a higher likelihood of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_quantifies_systemic_third_party_harm has no association with delta, controlling for any_comment_asserts_propositional_falsity.
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_quantifies_systemic_third_party_harm is positively associated with delta, controlling for any_comment_asserts_propositional_falsity.
hypotheses.note: The claim's "rather than" contrast is approximated by the harm coefficient adjusting for the falsity indicator; the two are not mutually exclusive, and the coefficient is not an exclusive harm-vs-falsity comparison. "Any comment" is used because the hypothesis does not specify a frequency; discussion-level scope is taken as the OC_comments only. Systemic harm vs individual harm boundary is semantic judgment.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments identify logical contradictions within the original post's own stated premises are associated with higher view-change rates than those citing external evidence.
hypotheses.h0: Coefficient of any_comment_identifies_op_premise_contradiction equals that of any_comment_cites_external_evidence in predicting view change (no difference).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_identifies_op_premise_contradiction have higher view-change rates than those with any_comment_cites_external_evidence.
hypotheses.note: Claim is a contrast between two groups (contradiction vs external evidence); the two features are not mutually exclusive and the OLS coefficients beta_A and beta_B are separate, so no single available coefficient represents beta_A - beta_B; term=null. A difference test would need a contrast of the two coefficients. Comment order is unspecified; features are discussion-level any-indicators; mixed discussions overlap.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments provide specific factual data or verifiable citations are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_specific_data_or_citation has no association with the likelihood of the OP changing their view (delta).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_specific_data_or_citation is associated with a higher likelihood of the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis says "counter-arguments provide" without a frequency rule, so "any comment" is used. Binary outcome is modeled with OLS (linear probability). Associational only. Comment order and chronology are unknown.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains explicit polite apology phrases are associated with a lower likelihood of view change compared to arguments without such phrases.
hypotheses.h0: op_argument_has_polite_apology has no association with the likelihood of view change (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: op_argument_has_polite_apology is associated with a lower likelihood of view change (coefficient < 0).
hypotheses.note: Uses current argument text (including marked edits); no initial snapshot. Linear probability model on binary delta. Apology phrase list is illustrative, not exhaustive.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Original posts featuring first-person vulnerable admissions are associated with higher view-change likelihood than those containing distant, third-person observations.
hypotheses.h0: Holding op_distant_third_person_observation fixed, op_first_person_vulnerable_admission has no association with view-change (delta) likelihood.
hypotheses.h1: Holding op_distant_third_person_observation fixed, posts with op_first_person_vulnerable_admission have higher view-change likelihood.
hypotheses.note: The two features can overlap, and the claim contrasts vulnerable posts with distant-observation posts. The coefficient on the vulnerable-admission feature, controlling for the observation feature, only approximates that contrast. It does not isolate posts that contain only one type. The OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments include direct URLs or external links are associated with a higher likelihood of view change than those solely using internal text.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_has_external_link has no association with the probability of view change (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_has_external_link = 1 have a higher probability of view change than those with 0 (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: Comparison group is discussions with no detected link in counter-arguments (interpreted as 'solely internal text'). Regex detects only explicit URLs/www links; bare domains without scheme are missed. OLS on a binary outcome is a linear probability model. Comment text may have had links stripped or altered at collection.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments employ specific, verifiable procedural examples are associated with higher original post view-change rates than those relying solely on abstract theoretical rebuttals.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with any_comment_specific_verifiable_procedural_example=1 have the same view-change rate as discussions with all_comments_solely_abstract_theoretical_rebuttal=1.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_specific_verifiable_procedural_example=1 have a higher view-change rate than discussions with all_comments_solely_abstract_theoretical_rebuttal=1.
hypotheses.note: The claim contrasts procedural-example discussions with solely-abstract ones. With both indicators, they are nearly complementary for non-empty rows, so beta_A alone does not equal the contrast beta_A - beta_B, and no single coefficient represents it. Because of that, term is null. Empty comment lists are not possible in this data (min 1 comment). "Verifiable" is judged from the supplied text only. Delta is only the outcome.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains specific counter-question markers are associated with a higher probability of view change.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with op_argument_has_counter_question=1 have the same probability of view change as those with 0.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with op_argument_has_counter_question=1 have a higher probability of view change than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: "Specific counter-question markers" is not defined in the hypothesis; operationalized as the presence of any counter-question in the OP argument (not a fixed marker list). The binary outcome is modeled with OLS (linear probability model). The current argument text is used, which may include edits.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original poster's argument includes personal anecdotes or first-person experiential narratives are associated with a lower likelihood of view change.
hypotheses.h0: op_has_personal_anecdote has no association with likelihood of view change (delta).
hypotheses.h1: op_has_personal_anecdote is associated with a lower likelihood of view change (delta).
hypotheses.note: Uses current argument text, including any marked edits; no initial snapshot is available. Linear probability model on binary delta; no controls added.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly acknowledge the validity of the original post's initial premise before introducing divergence are associated with a higher likelihood of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_acknowledges_premise_validity_before_divergence has no association with view change (delta) probability.
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_acknowledges_premise_validity_before_divergence is positively associated with view change probability.
hypotheses.note: Hypothesis says "counter-arguments" without specifying any vs. all or frequency; "any comment" chosen, no frequency cutoff invented. Ordering within a comment is judged from text order. OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model. "Initial" premise is read from supplied current OP text; no initial snapshot is available.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments employ concrete personal anecdotes are more likely associated with the original poster changing their view than those using abstract reasoning.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_concrete_personal_anecdote and any_comment_abstract_reasoning have equal associations with delta (anecdote coefficient equals abstract coefficient).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_concrete_personal_anecdote have higher probability of delta than those relying on any_comment_abstract_reasoning (anecdote coefficient greater than abstract coefficient).
hypotheses.note: The claim contrasts anecdote vs abstract reasoning (beta_A - beta_B), which is not a single design-matrix coefficient in this model, so term is null; the individual coefficients would not test the comparison. The features are not mutually exclusive (a discussion can have both). No frequency or dominance rule is specified for 'employ'; any-comment is used. Comment list order carries no chronology.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing at least three distinct counter-argument comments are associated with a higher probability of the original poster changing their view than those with fewer.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with has_three_plus_oc_comments = 1 have the same probability of OP view change as those with has_three_plus_oc_comments = 0.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with has_three_plus_oc_comments = 1 have a higher probability of OP view change than those with has_three_plus_oc_comments = 0.
hypotheses.note: "Distinct" operationalized as separate entries in OC_comments; no semantic deduplication of arguments. OC_comments may be a subset of the full discussion (observed counts 1-17, mostly 1), so the count reflects supplied comments only. Linear probability model on binary delta.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Posts containing direct counterarguments are more likely to result in the original poster upvoting the reply or changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: any_direct_counterargument has no association with the probability that the OP changes their view.
hypotheses.h1: Posts with any_direct_counterargument=1 have a higher probability of OP view change than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: Only view change (delta) is available as outcome; OP upvoting a reply is not observed. Dataset comments are all counter-argument comments, so the feature may have little variance. Linear probability model via OLS.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument employs modest or uncertain epistemic markers are associated with a higher likelihood of view change than those using high-modality assertions.
hypotheses.h0: Likelihood of view change does not differ between discussions with op_argument_uncertain_markers and those with op_argument_high_modality_assertion.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with op_argument_uncertain_markers have a higher likelihood of view change than those with op_argument_high_modality_assertion.
hypotheses.note: The claim contrasts uncertain vs high-modality groups, i.e. beta_uncertain minus beta_high, which is not a single coefficient in this OLS (each coefficient is versus the neutral baseline), so term is null. Predominance of markers is an unspecified boundary left to the annotator; no initial-snapshot restriction is stated, so current text is used.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains explicit tone-policing requests are associated with a lower likelihood of view change compared to those without such requests.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with op_explicit_tone_policing_request = 1 have the same likelihood of view change as those with 0.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with op_explicit_tone_policing_request = 1 have a lower likelihood of view change than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: Tone-policing is operationalized as the OP's explicit request in the argument text (current text, including edits; no initial snapshot). Likely rare in the data. Linear probability model via OLS.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments utilize a redrafting strategy, rewriting the original poster's viewpoint from a nuanced perspective before refutation, are associated with higher view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_redrafts_op_view_before_refuting has no association with view change (delta).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_redrafts_op_view_before_refuting is positively associated with view change (delta).
hypotheses.note: The claim does not say any vs. share of comments; "any comment" was chosen as the discussion-level reading. "Nuanced" is judged semantically with no fixed cutoff. OLS on a binary outcome is a linear probability model. No controls are added.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the observed original-post score exceeds 50 are associated with a lower likelihood of view change than those with lower observed scores.
hypotheses.h0: Post_score_above_50 has no association with the likelihood of view change (delta).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with post_score_above_50 = 1 have a lower likelihood of view change than those with post_score_above_50 = 0.
hypotheses.note: Score is observed at collection time (may be affected by later events); OLS on binary outcome is a linear probability model. Threshold 50 is strict (>50).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original poster's argument contains explicit uncertainty markers are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with op_argument_has_explicit_uncertainty = 1 have the same likelihood of OP view change as those with 0 (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with op_argument_has_explicit_uncertainty = 1 have a higher likelihood of OP view change (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: Uses current argument text including marked edits; no initial snapshot is available. OLS on binary outcome (linear probability model). 'Explicit uncertainty markers' has no fixed lexicon or frequency cutoff; any qualifying marker suffices.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original poster's initial argument explicitly acknowledges a counter-argument or limitation are directionally associated with a higher probability of view change.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with op_acknowledges_counterargument_or_limitation=1 have the same probability of view change as those with 0.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with op_acknowledges_counterargument_or_limitation=1 have a higher probability of view change than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis restricts to the OP's initial argument, but only current text (with possibly edited content) is supplied and no initial snapshot exists; edits may add acknowledgments after replies. Faithful testing is not possible, so term is null. The feature measures current supplied text, and the rhs is listed only for reference.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Counter-arguments containing named, real-world analogies (e.g., specific historical or scientific examples) are associated with higher view-change rates than abstract logical rebuttals.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_named_real_world_analogy and any_comment_abstract_logical_rebuttal have equal associations with view-change rate (no higher rate for named analogies than abstract rebuttals).
hypotheses.h1: View-change rate is higher for any_comment_named_real_world_analogy than for any_comment_abstract_logical_rebuttal.
hypotheses.note: The claim is a contrast (named analogy vs abstract rebuttal), i.e. beta_A - beta_B, which is not a single coefficient in this OLS; no single term represents it, so term is null. Rows can have both types or neither, so the groups overlap and are not exclusive. Comment-level attribution of delta is unavailable (row-level outcome). Analogy-vs-abstract classification is subjective.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly contrast the original poster's view with a relatable real-world personal experience are associated with a higher likelihood of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_contrasts_op_view_with_personal_experience has no association with delta (coefficient = 0).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_contrasts_op_view_with_personal_experience has a positive association with delta (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: "Relatable" is subjective; judged by the annotator. Outcome delta is binary, tested via OLS (linear probability). The hypothesis does not specify any vs. all comments; "any" was chosen as the natural reading.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussion posts with titles containing explicit emotional or personal identifiers are associated with a lower likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: title_explicit_emotional_or_personal_identifier has no association with the probability of the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.h1: title_explicit_emotional_or_personal_identifier is associated with a lower probability of the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis does not define 'emotional or personal identifiers' precisely; the operationalization is a broad interpretation. OLS on binary outcome is a linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing multi-turn reply interactions in the conversation text are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: Rows with has_multi_turn_reply_interaction=1 have the same likelihood of OP view change as rows with 0 (coefficient on has_multi_turn_reply_interaction = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Rows with has_multi_turn_reply_interaction=1 have higher likelihood of OP view change (coefficient > 0).
hypotheses.note: Conversation may include later replies and view-change announcements (leakage); the feature is defined only on interaction structure and must not use delta-related content. Binary outcome modeled with OLS (linear probability). Turn attribution relies on '[user]:' formatting; the OP's participation is not separately identified.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Posts containing a single, highly-rated counterargument are associated with an increased frequency of attribution replies from the original poster.
hypotheses.h0: Posts with exactly one counterargument that is highly rated do not differ in frequency of OP attribution replies from other posts; this cannot be tested with the available features.
hypotheses.h1: Posts with a single highly-rated counterargument have a higher frequency of OP attribution replies; this cannot be tested with the available features.
hypotheses.note: Not faithfully testable. (1) No comment ratings/scores exist in the data (post_score is the OP post's score, not a comment rating), so 'highly-rated' cannot be measured. It is also an unspecified boundary. (2) The outcome, frequency of OP attribution replies, is not a dataset column. The outcome delta is a different construct. OP replies appear only in conversation, which is leakage-prone, has no reliable OP identity and is not a clean count. (3) The supplied code features capture only the 'single comment' cardinality and are not a proxy for the claim. The rhs is a placeholder and no coefficient represents the hypothesis, so term=null.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains explicit self-referential meta-commentary regarding platform mechanics or author status are associated with a lower probability of view change.
hypotheses.h0: op_self_meta_commentary_platform_or_status has no association with probability of view change.
hypotheses.h1: op_self_meta_commentary_platform_or_status is associated with lower probability of view change.
hypotheses.note: Uses supplied current argument text, including marked edits; no initial snapshot is available. Construct boundaries between status and platform meta-commentary rely on the prompt's wording. Edits may include post-hoc meta-commentary (e.g., delta notes) that is counted as current text.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-argument comments include direct quotes from the original argument are more frequently associated with a changed view than those without such quotations.
hypotheses.h0: Mean delta does not differ between rows with any_comment_quotes_op_argument=1 and =0.
hypotheses.h1: Rows with any_comment_quotes_op_argument=1 have higher probability of a changed view (delta) than rows with 0.
hypotheses.note: Association only, linear probability model. Quote detection uses current argument text, including edits; OP-edit timing is unknown. Comment list order carries no chronology.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Posts with observed scores below the median are associated with a lower probability of the original poster changing their view compared to higher-scored posts.

hypotheses.h1: Posts with post_score_below_median = 1 have a lower probability of OP view change than posts with post_score_below_median = 0.
hypotheses.note: Median is the dataset-wide median of post_score (7); posts equal to the median are grouped with higher-scored posts, since the claim does not specify tie handling. Score is observed at collection and may be affected by the outcome; association only. OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments use second-person direct address to the original poster are associated with a higher likelihood of view change.

hypotheses.h1: any_comment_second_person_address_to_op is associated with a higher likelihood of view change (delta).
hypotheses.note: Interpreted "discussions where counter-arguments use second-person address" as any comment doing so; the hypothesis gives no frequency rule. Association only; OLS on binary outcome (linear probability model). Impersonal generic 'you' is excluded, which requires judgment.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original poster's argument contains a direct plea for non-violация are associated with a lower likelihood of view change.

hypotheses.note: Hypothesis term was garbled ('non-violация'); interpreted as non-violence. Binary outcome modeled with OLS (linear probability). The plea is likely rare, limiting power. No controls added per claim.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument contains explicit first-person singular pronouns are associated with a higher probability of view change.
hypotheses.h0: op_argument_has_first_person_singular has no association with the probability of view change (coefficient = 0).

hypotheses.note: Regex approximates pronoun detection; Roman numeral/list 'I' may produce false positives. Linear probability model via OLS on binary delta. Current text including edits is used, no initial snapshot.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The presence of a logged counterargument is positively associated with the probability that the original poster posts a viewpoint change or awards a delta.
hypotheses.h0: has_counterargument_comment has no association with the probability of delta/viewpoint change.
hypotheses.h1: has_counterargument_comment is positively associated with the probability of delta/viewpoint change.
hypotheses.note: In the data, every row has at least 1 comment in OC_comments (min 1, none empty), so the predictor is constant (all 1). The coefficient is not identifiable and the hypothesis cannot be tested on this dataset, because there is no comparison group with no counterargument. "Logged" is read as present in OC_comments. The model is a linear probability model via OLS.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Higher cognitive complexity in counterarguments is associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their stated view in ChangeMyView discussions.

hypotheses.h1: Higher counterargument_cognitive_complexity is associated with a higher likelihood of the OP changing their view.
hypotheses.note: Cognitive complexity has no specified operationalization in the hypothesis; the 0-10 rubric is an operational choice, not a validated instrument. Scored over all counterarguments jointly (aggregation is not specified in the claim). OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly acknowledge the original poster's underlying valid point before introducing the discrepancy are associated with higher view-change rates than pure refutations.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions where any_comment_acknowledges_valid_point_before_disagreement is 1 have the same view-change rate as those where it is 0 (pure refutations).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions where any_comment_acknowledges_valid_point_before_disagreement is 1 have higher view-change rates than those where it is 0.
hypotheses.note: The 0 group includes all discussions without such acknowledgment, not strictly verified 'pure refutations'; no separate pure-refutation construct was defined. Delta is binary, so the OLS is a linear probability model. The hypothesis does not say whether acknowledgment must be in all comments, so 'any' was used.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments reference specific, named external programs or locations are associated with higher view-change rates than those using only abstract logical refutation.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_names_specific_program_or_location has no association with view-change rate (delta).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_names_specific_program_or_location = 1 have higher view-change rates than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: The claimed comparator is "only abstract logical refutation"; the feature's 0 group is "no named program/location", which may include non-abstract discussions (e.g., anecdotes or unnamed examples) and is only an approximate comparator. No separate abstract-only feature was defined to avoid inventing an undeclared semantic category. Comment order is not chronology.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly quote and refute specific phrases from the original post are associated with a higher likelihood of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_quotes_and_refutes_op_phrase has no association with the likelihood of view change (delta).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_quotes_and_refutes_op_phrase is positively associated with the likelihood of view change.
hypotheses.note: Hypothesis wording "counter-arguments" is read as any comment in the row (no frequency cutoff given). OLS on binary outcome is a linear probability model. Comment order/chronology unavailable.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly refute specific examples or anecdotes provided by the original poster are associated with a higher probability of view change compared to arguments addressing the main premise directly.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_refutes_op_example has no association with view change probability relative to any_comment_addresses_main_premise.
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_refutes_op_example have higher view change probability than those with any_comment_addresses_main_premise.
hypotheses.note: The claim is a contrast (example refutation vs premise-addressing); it requires beta_example - beta_premise, which is not a single design-matrix coefficient, so term is null. The two features are not mutually exclusive (a discussion can have both) and the claim's comparison group is imperfectly defined at the discussion level. OLS on binary outcome is a linear probability model. Comment order is not chronology.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the original argument uses hedging or qualifying language are associated with a higher likelihood of view change than those using absolute declarative statements.
hypotheses.h0: Controlling for op_argument_uses_absolute_statements, op_argument_uses_hedging has no association with delta.
hypotheses.h1: Controlling for op_argument_uses_absolute_statements, op_argument_uses_hedging is positively associated with delta.
hypotheses.note: Hedging and absolute statements are not mutually exclusive, so the claimed contrast (hedged vs absolute-declarative arguments) is only approximated; the hedging coefficient is net of absolute statements, not an exact hedged-only vs absolute-only comparison. Binary presence, no frequency cutoff specified. Outcome is delta, added automatically (OLS linear probability).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly quote the original poster's text rather than paraphrasing are associated with a higher probability of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_quotes_op_text has no association with probability of view change.
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_quotes_op_text is positively associated with probability of view change.
hypotheses.note: The comparison group is discussions with no explicit quoting of OP text (which may paraphrase or not); paraphrase use is not separately measured, so quoting vs paraphrasing is only approximated by quote presence vs absence. Linear probability model via OLS.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing counter-arguments that explicitly validate the original poster's emotional experience prior to logical rebuttal are associated with higher view-change rates.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_validates_op_emotion_before_rebuttal has no association with view-change rate (delta).
hypotheses.h1: Discussions with any_comment_validates_op_emotion_before_rebuttal = 1 have a higher view-change rate.
hypotheses.note: Hypothesis says "counter-arguments" (plural) without a frequency rule; operationalized as any comment. Order within a comment is judged from text; list order is not used. Linear probability model on binary delta.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing counter-arguments that use analogies to familiar scenarios are associated with a higher likelihood of the original poster changing their view.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_uses_familiar_analogy has no association with the probability of OP view change (delta).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_uses_familiar_analogy is associated with a higher probability of OP view change.
hypotheses.note: Association only, OLS linear probability model on binary delta. "Familiar" is judged by the annotator without a fixed list. Analogy scope is over OC_comments only, not later replies.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where the title explicitly contains an absolute universal quantifier like 'all' or 'never' are associated with lower view change than those using variable or probabilistic terms.

hypotheses.note: The claim contrasts absolute vs variable titles, i.e. beta_abs - beta_var, which is not a single design-matrix coefficient; each coefficient is relative to the neither-term baseline, so term is null. Titles with both term types are coded 1 on both. Term lists are nonexhaustive and judged semantically.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing counter-arguments that explicitly reference specific, concrete examples or real-world instances in the provided comments are associated with a higher probability of view change.
hypotheses.h0: any_comment_concrete_real_world_example has zero association with probability of view change (delta).
hypotheses.h1: any_comment_concrete_real_world_example is positively associated with probability of view change.
hypotheses.note: Hypothesis says "discussions containing" such comments, operationalized as any comment. OLS on binary delta is a linear probability model. Comments are only the supplied ones; no chronology.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments contain specific empirical evidence are more likely to be associated with the original poster changing their view than those containing only logical refutations.
hypotheses.h0: Discussions with any_comment_specific_empirical_evidence=1 have the same probability of OP view change as discussions with only_logical_refutation_comments=1.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly acknowledge the validity of a specific component of the original argument before presenting a counter-example are associated with higher view change rates.

hypotheses.h1: Discussions with ack_component_before_counterexample = 1 have a higher view change rate than those with 0.
hypotheses.note: Any-comment interpretation; hypothesis does not specify frequency. Binary outcome modeled with OLS (linear probability). Comment order is unknown, so acknowledgment-before-counterexample is judged only within a single comment.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments utilize second-person direct address are associated with higher original poster view-change rates than arguments relying on third-person analysis.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly introduce verifiable external facts distinct from the original argument are associated with a higher probability of view change.

hypotheses.h1: op_acknowledges_alternative_perspectives is positively associated with likelihood of view change.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing multiple distinct counter-argument comments are associated with a higher likelihood of view change than those containing only a single comment.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Counter-arguments frequently embedding direct quotations from the original post are associated with a higher likelihood of view change than those lacking explicit textual anchoring.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing counter-arguments with specific real-world examples are associated with a higher probability of original poster view change than those lacking such citations.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments contain concrete real-world examples are associated with higher original-poster view change rates than those relying solely on abstract logic.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions containing counter-arguments that cite specific real-world examples are associated with a higher probability of the original poster changing their view.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Discussions where counter-arguments explicitly challenge the original poster's underlying assumptions rather than just their factual conclusions are associated with higher view-change rates.

feature.name: any_comment_relies_on_abstract_normative_principles
feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments): any comment relies on abstract normative principles (general moral/ethical/political principles or values) as its argument basis.
feature.spec: Read OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than the OP). Return 1 if at least one comment argues mainly by appeal to abstract normative principles (general moral, ethical, rights, justice, fairness or value principles stated in general terms) rather than a specific concrete example. Return 0 if no comment does. A comment may also cite precedents; count it only if abstract normative principles are a substantial basis of its argument. Empty list gives 0; missing or malformed gives null. Do not use other columns.

feature.name: all_comments_solely_abstract_normative
feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments): every comment relies solely on abstract normative principles, with no concrete personal labor-process details.
feature.spec: Read the OC_comments JSON list (comments by users other than the OP; ignore order). Return 1 if the list is nonempty and the counter-arguments rely solely on abstract normative principles (general claims about what is right, fair, or ought to be, e.g. rights, justice, duty) and none introduces concrete personal or specific labor-process details or other concrete examples. Return 0 if any comment contains concrete details or non-normative argumentation. Exclude quoted text from others and bot/moderator notices unless adopted. Valid empty list -> null; missing or malformed OC_comments -> null.

comparisons.reason: Different quantifiers and null rules. Item 0 is an 'any' measure: 1 if at least one comment mainly appeals to abstract normative principles, and an empty list gives 0. Item 1 is an 'all/solely' measure: 1 only if the list is nonempty and every comment is purely abstract normative with no concrete details or non-normative argumentation, and an empty list gives null. Item 1 also adds explicit exclusions for quoted text and bot notices. Any versus all, and the empty-list handling (0 versus null), are material differences.

feature.name: op_explicit_uncertainty_admission
feature.definition: OP's own argument text (post body): 1 if the OP explicitly admits uncertainty or possible error in their own view
feature.spec: Read only the argument column (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if the OP, in their own voice, explicitly expresses uncertainty about their view or admits they could be wrong or lack knowledge (e.g. 'I'm not sure', 'I may be wrong', 'I could be mistaken'). Exclude quoted external text, opponents' positions reported by the OP, and moderator/bot notices unless the OP adopts them. Generic hedging words without an explicit admission do not count. Return 0 if the argument is present and has no such admission. Return null if argument is missing or malformed.

feature.name: op_argument_uncertain_markers
feature.definition: OP argument text (post body, current text incl. marked edits, excluding quoted others' text): 1 if the OP's own claims are expressed with modest or uncertain epistemic markers
feature.spec: Read only the argument column (OP post body, current text including marked edits). Ignore quoted text from others and non-OP material. Return 1 if the OP's own stance/claims are predominantly framed with modest or uncertain epistemic markers (e.g. hedges, tentative modals, expressions of doubt or possible error, 'I think maybe', 'might', 'not sure'); examples are nonexhaustive. Return 0 if the OP's own claims are not predominantly so framed (including predominantly high-modality assertion or neutral). Null if argument is missing, empty or unreadable.

comparisons.reason: Feature 0 is an any-presence test for an explicit admission of uncertainty or possible error, and it says generic hedging words alone do not count. Feature 30 asks whether the OP's claims are predominantly framed with modest or uncertain epistemic markers. Hedges and tentative modals count there, and it is a predominance judgment. One explicit 'I may be wrong' would give 1 for feature 0 but could give 0 for feature 30. Heavy hedging with no explicit admission would give 0 for feature 0 and 1 for feature 30. The eligibility rules, the any-versus-predominant threshold and the null rules (malformed input versus empty or unreadable) also differ.

feature.name: op_explicit_uncertainty_admission
feature.definition: OP's own argument text (post body): 1 if the OP explicitly admits uncertainty or possible error in their own view
feature.spec: Read only the argument column (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if the OP, in their own voice, explicitly expresses uncertainty about their view or admits they could be wrong or lack knowledge (e.g. 'I'm not sure', 'I may be wrong', 'I could be mistaken'). Exclude quoted external text, opponents' positions reported by the OP, and moderator/bot notices unless the OP adopts them. Generic hedging words without an explicit admission do not count. Return 0 if the argument is present and has no such admission. Return null if argument is missing or malformed.

feature.name: op_argument_has_explicit_uncertainty
feature.definition: OP argument text (post body, current text incl. marked edits; excluding quotations of others): 1 if the OP expresses explicit uncertainty markers about their own view or claims, else 0
feature.spec: Read the 'argument' column (OP's post body, current text including marked edits). Output 1 if the OP, in their own voice, explicitly marks uncertainty about their own view or claims (e.g. 'I'm not sure', 'I might be wrong', 'maybe', 'I could be mistaken', 'to my knowledge', 'I don't know whether'). Output 0 if no such explicit marker appears. Ignore quoted text from others, reported opponents' positions, and moderator/bot notices unless the OP adopts them as their own uncertainty. Generic hedging words not signalling uncertainty about the OP's own stance do not count; absolute certainty is not required for 0 beyond absence of markers. Do not use title, comments or other columns. Return null if argument is missing or empty/malformed.

comparisons.reason: Both read the argument column only with the same attribution rules, but the predicates differ in breadth. Item 0 needs an explicit admission of uncertainty, possible error or lack of knowledge, and generic hedging words without an explicit admission do not count. Item 1 counts any explicit uncertainty marker, and its examples include bare 'maybe' and 'to my knowledge', which item 0 would exclude as generic hedging. The null rules also differ: item 0 returns null only if the argument is missing or malformed, while item 1 also returns null if it is empty. So item 1 is a broader, marker-based measure and the two are not the same row function.

feature.name: op_asserts_absolute_certainty
feature.definition: OP's own argument text (post body): 1 if the OP explicitly asserts absolute certainty or that their view cannot be wrong
feature.spec: Read only the argument column (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if the OP, in their own voice, explicitly asserts absolute certainty about their view (e.g. 'I am 100% certain', 'there is no possible way I'm wrong', 'undeniably true'). Merely confident or opinionated tone does not count. Exclude quoted external text and reported opponents' positions. Return 0 if argument is present and has no such assertion. Return null if argument is missing or malformed.

feature.name: op_argument_uses_absolute_statements
feature.definition: OP argument text (post body, current text incl. marked edits; excluding quoted external text): 1 if the OP makes absolute declarative statements stated as unqualified certainties
feature.spec: Read the 'argument' column only. Return 1 if the OP, in their own voice, makes at least one absolute declarative statement: a claim asserted flatly as certain or universal without qualification (e.g. 'always', 'never', 'everyone', 'obviously', 'it is a fact that', or a bare categorical assertion); examples nonexhaustive. Ignore quoted external text. Use the current text including marked edits. Return 0 if assessable and none present. Return null if argument is missing or empty/malformed. Independent of hedging: both features may be 1 for the same row.

comparisons.reason: Feature 0 requires an explicit assertion of absolute certainty about the OP's own view (e.g. 'I am 100% certain', 'cannot be wrong'), and tone alone doesn't count. Feature 1 fires on any single flat universal or categorical declarative statement ('always', 'never', 'everyone', 'obviously', or a bare categorical assertion), about any content. Feature 1 is much broader, so a row with 'everyone does X' scores 1 on feature 1 and 0 on feature 0. Feature 1's spec also states the two can differ for the same row. Feature 1 also returns null for empty arguments, and feature 0 doesn't state that rule.

feature.name: op_asserts_absolute_certainty
feature.definition: OP's own argument text (post body): 1 if the OP explicitly asserts absolute certainty or that their view cannot be wrong
feature.spec: Read only the argument column (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if the OP, in their own voice, explicitly asserts absolute certainty about their view (e.g. 'I am 100% certain', 'there is no possible way I'm wrong', 'undeniably true'). Merely confident or opinionated tone does not count. Exclude quoted external text and reported opponents' positions. Return 0 if argument is present and has no such assertion. Return null if argument is missing or malformed.

feature.name: op_argument_unwavering_certainty
feature.definition: OP argument text: 1 if the OP presents their view with unwavering certainty, with no explicit hedging or self-doubt markers, else 0
feature.spec: Read only the argument column (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if the OP presents their own view with unwavering certainty: assertive, categorical framing and no explicit hedging, tentativeness, or self-doubt about their own view in their own voice (ignore hedges within quoted others' text). Return 0 if the argument contains any explicit hedging or self-doubt marker, or is merely neutral/non-assertive without being categorical. Return null if argument is missing or empty/malformed. Do not use any other column.

comparisons.reason: Feature 0 requires an explicit assertion of absolute certainty or that the view can't be wrong (e.g. '100% certain'), and returns 0 for anything lacking it. Feature 70 is a broader, different predicate: categorical assertive framing plus the absence of any hedging or self-doubt. A confident post with no hedges and no explicit certainty claim gets 0 on feature 0 but 1 on feature 70. Their 0 rules also differ: feature 70 gives 0 for any hedge, even when the OP also makes a certainty claim. Their null rules differ too, since 70 also nulls on an empty argument.

feature.name: any_comment_cites_specific_real_world_example
feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments): 1 if any comment explicitly cites a specific real-world example in support of its argument, else 0
feature.spec: Read OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than the OP; order carries no meaning). Output 1 if at least one comment explicitly cites a specific real-world example (a particular identifiable real event, person, case, organization, place, study, product or concrete documented instance, not a purely hypothetical, generic or vague 'some people' reference) as support for its argument. Named examples in the construct are nonexhaustive; no external verification is required. Quotes of others do not count unless the commenter uses them as a specific example. Output 0 if the list is valid and no comment does so. Empty list gives 0; missing or malformed input gives null.

feature.name: any_comment_concrete_real_world_example
feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments): any comment provides a concrete real-world example (specific real-world case, instance, event, person, or documented situation) in support of its argument
feature.spec: Read the OC_comments JSON list (comments by users other than OP). Return 1 if at least one comment provides a concrete real-world example, i.e. a specific actual case, instance, event, person, organization, statistic-bearing situation or personal real-life experience used to support its point. Return 0 if the list is valid and nonempty but no comment does so (purely abstract reasoning, hypotheticals, or generic claims). Hypothetical/invented scenarios do not count. Do not require external verification. Examples are nonexhaustive. Ignore the conversation column and any OP replies. Return 0 for a valid empty list; null if OC_comments is missing or malformed.

comparisons.reason: Both are binary any-comment flags over OC_comments only. Each requires a specific, actual real-world example (event, person, case, organization and so on) used to support the comment's argument. Both exclude hypothetical, generic or vague references and require no external verification. Both return 0 for a valid empty list and null for missing or malformed input. Spec 1 adds 'statistic-bearing situation' and 'personal real-life experience', and spec 0 adds 'study, product, place'. These are ordinary nonexhaustive example lists, and both require a specific actual instance, so they are not material differences. Spec 0 says quotes of others don't count unless used as an example. Spec 1 doesn't mention quotes but its 'used to support its point' condition covers the same case. Spec 1's 'ignore conversation column and OP replies' matches the OC_comments-only source in spec 0.

feature.name: any_comment_cites_specific_real_world_example
feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments): 1 if any comment explicitly cites a specific real-world example in support of its argument, else 0
feature.spec: Read OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than the OP; order carries no meaning). feature.name: any_comment_specific_data_or_citation
feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments, not OP): 1 if any comment provides specific factual data or verifiable citations, else 0
feature.spec: Read the JSON list in OC_comments (comments by users other than the OP; ignore order). Return 1 if at least one comment itself supplies specific factual data (e.g., concrete statistics, figures, dates, named studies or documented specifics) or verifiable citations/references (e.g., links, named sources, studies, laws, publications) in support of its points. Vague appeals to unspecified facts or 'studies show' without specifics, opinions, and hypotheticals do not count. Quoted text from the OP does not count. Return 0 if the list is valid and no comment qualifies. Return null if OC_comments is missing or malformed. Empty valid list gives 0. Use only current supplied text.

comparisons.reason: Both are any-comment binary features over OC_comments, but the constructs differ. Feature 0 requires a specific real-world example (an identifiable event, person, case, organization, place or product) cited in support of an argument. Feature 1 requires specific factual data (statistics, figures, dates) or verifiable citations (links, named sources, laws). A comment can give a named example with no data or citation, such as naming a historical event or a company. A comment can also give a statistic or a law citation without a particular real-world case. The overlap is partial, so the eligibility rules differ materially.

feature.name: any_comment_concrete_personal_anecdote
feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments, not the OP): 1 if any comment employs a concrete personal anecdote, else 0.
feature.spec: Read the OC_comments JSON list (comments by users other than the OP; ignore conversation and later replies). Return 1 if at least one comment uses a concrete personal anecdote, i.e. the commenter recounts a specific experience of their own or someone they personally know (particular events, people, or situations) as part of their counter-argument. Quoted text from others, hypotheticals, generic statistics and general claims do not count. Return 0 if the list is valid and no comment does. Return null if OC_comments is missing or malformed. Empty valid list gives 0.

comparisons.reason: Different constructs. Feature 0 is 1 for any specific identifiable real-world example (event, person, case, organization, study, product or documented instance) cited as support. Feature 1 is 1 only for a commenter's own or a personal acquaintance's specific experience. Feature 0 includes public cases and studies that feature 1 excludes. Feature 1 includes private personal experiences that feature 0 doesn't require to be identifiable or documented. The sources and the null and empty rules match, but the eligibility rules differ materially.

feature.spec: Read OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than the OP) jointly with the OP title and argument (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if at least one comment explicitly quotes (e.g., quoted or blockquoted text matching/paraphrasing closely the OP's wording) or explicitly references a specific identifiable textual element of the OP's title/argument (a particular sentence, phrase, claim, example or passage, e.g. 'you said X', 'your point about Y'). Endorsement/agreement is not required; the quote/reference itself counts. Merely addressing the general topic or the view overall without pointing to specific OP text does not count. Return 0 if the list is valid and nonempty and no comment does so, provided title/argument are available. Return null if OC_comments is missing/malformed or empty-of-parse, or if OP title/argument is missing so absence cannot be established (a clear positive quote may still yield 1). Do not use the conversation column or later replies. Output 0/1/null.

comparisons.reason: Different constructs. Feature 0 needs a comment to refute (argue against or debunk) a specific OP example or anecdote in the body. Feature 1 needs only that a comment quotes or references any specific OP text element, and endorsement or disagreement is not required. A quote or reference is not a refutation, and feature 1 covers any phrase, claim or sentence rather than only examples. The empty-list rules also differ: feature 0 returns 0 for an empty list, while feature 1 returns null.

feature.definition: OP argument text (post body, current text incl. marked edits; excluding quoted external text): 1 if the OP uses hedging or qualifying language in their own assertions
feature.spec: Read the 'argument' column only. Return 1 if the OP, in their own voice, uses hedging or qualifying language that softens or limits the strength of a claim (e.g. 'I think', 'maybe', 'perhaps', 'in most cases', 'might', 'to my knowledge', 'generally'); these are nonexhaustive examples. Ignore hedges inside quotations of others or in non-claim text. Use the current text including marked edits. Return 0 if the argument is assessable and has no such language. Return null if argument is missing or empty/malformed.

feature.name: op_argument_has_hedging_or_self_doubt

feature.spec: Read only the argument column (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if the OP, in their own voice, uses at least one explicit hedging or self-doubt marker about their own view/claims (e.g. 'I might be wrong', 'I'm not sure', 'maybe', 'I could be missing something', 'it seems to me', 'I'm unsure'). Exclude hedges inside quotations of others, reported opposing positions, and generic non-OP text. Return 0 if the argument is assessable and has no such marker. Return null if argument is missing or empty/malformed. Do not use any other column.

comparisons.reason: Same source (argument) and 0/1/null rules, but the constructs differ in breadth. Feature 0 counts any hedging or qualifying language that softens or limits a claim, including quantifier or scope qualifiers such as 'in most cases', 'generally', 'to my knowledge'. Feature 1 requires explicit hedging or self-doubt markers about the OP's own view, such as 'I might be wrong' or 'I'm not sure'. Feature 0 is therefore broader and would score 1 on a generic qualifier like 'generally' that is not self-doubt. Feature 1 also restricts the target to the OP's view. Their exclusions are also worded differently.

feature_pairs.review_reason: Feature 0 is an any-presence test for an explicit admission of uncertainty or possible error, and it says generic hedging words alone do not count. Feature 30 asks whether the OP's claims are predominantly framed with modest or uncertain epistemic markers. Hedges and tentative modals count there, and it is a predominance judgment. One explicit 'I may be wrong' would give 1 for feature 0 but could give 0 for feature 30. Heavy hedging with no explicit admission would give 0 for feature 0 and 1 for feature 30. The eligibility rules, the any-versus-predominant threshold and the null rules (malformed input versus empty or unreadable) also differ.

feature_pairs.review_reason: Both are all-comment binary flags over OC_comments with the same null rule, but they test different constructs. Left: every comment is refuting reasoning or evidence and none explicitly validates the OP's dignity or effort. Evidence is allowed, and the disqualifier is personal validation. Right: every comment uses only abstract logical reasoning (definitions, structure, principles) and none introduces a concrete external factual analogy or example. The disqualifier is concrete real-world examples. A comment citing concrete evidence passes on the left and fails on the right. feature_pairs.review_reason: Both are all-comments binary features over OC_comments, but they measure different constructs. Feature 0 requires every comment to rely solely on abstract normative principles (claims about what is right, fair or ought to be). It returns 0 for any concrete details or any non-normative argumentation, including logical or factual argument. Feature 1 requires only abstract logical refutation (definitions, logical structure, general principles). It returns 0 only for a concrete external factual analogy or example. A purely logical, non-normative comment gives 0 under feature 0 and 1 under feature 1. Their exclusion rules also differ: feature 0 excludes quoted text and bot/moderator notices, and feature 1 states no such exclusion.

feature_pairs.review_reason: Both are any-comment binary features on title, argument and OC_comments, and both require acknowledgment before divergence. The target of the acknowledgment differs. Feature 0 requires an explicit statement that the OP's initial premise, meaning the central starting claim or assumption, is valid, correct, reasonable or true. Feature 1 accepts any valid point, or any part of the OP's underlying view, so a narrower premise-specific acknowledgment is a subset of it. Feature 1 also requires that a disagreement actually follows in the same comment. Feature 0 only requires that the acknowledgment come before any divergence. The null rules differ as well: feature 0 returns null if title and argument are both missing, while feature 1 returns null if any needed OP context is missing.

feature_pairs.review_reason: Both are any-comment binary features on the same sources, but the requirements differ. Item 0 requires acknowledging validity of the OP's initial premise (the central starting claim) before any divergence or disagreement. Its divergence can be of any kind, including a blanket disagreement. Item 1 accepts validity of the OP's view or any point of it. It then requires a narrower, specific caveat, exception or qualification, and explicitly excludes blanket rejection. So a comment that concedes the premise and then disagrees broadly scores 1 under item 0 and 0 under item 1. A comment that concedes a minor point and then adds a caveat scores 1 under item 1 and may score 0 under item 0. Null rules also differ. Item 0 returns null if the OP title and argument are missing, or if the comment list is empty-unparseable. Item 1 returns null only if OC_comments is missing or malformed.

Left (30) returns 1 only if the OP's claims are predominantly framed with modest or uncertain epistemic markers, which is a density/predominance threshold. right_feature.spec: Read OC_comments (JSON list of comment strings by users other than OP), together with the OP title and argument (current text including marked edits). Return 1 if at least one comment explicitly quotes text from the OP's title or argument, i.e. reproduces OP wording verbatim or near-verbatim as a quotation (e.g. Reddit '>' blockquote or quotation marks) that matches the OP text. left_feature.definition: OP argument text (post body, current text incl. marked edits; excluding quotations of others): 1 if the OP expresses explicit uncertainty markers about their own view or claims, else 0
left_feature.spec: Read the 'argument' column (OP's post body, current text including marked edits). Output 1 if the OP, in their own voice, explicitly marks uncertainty about their own view or claims (e.g. 'I'm not sure', 'I might be wrong', 'maybe', 'I could be mistaken', 'to my knowledge', 'I don't know whether'). Do not use title, comments or other columns. Return null if argument is missing or empty/malformed.

right_feature.spec: Read OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than the OP) jointly with the OP title and argument (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if at least one comment explicitly quotes (e.g., quoted or blockquoted text matching/paraphrasing closely the OP's wording) or explicitly references a specific identifiable textual element of the OP's title/argument (a particular sentence, phrase, claim, example or passage, e.g. 'you said X', 'your point about Y'). Endorsement/agreement is not required; the quote/reference itself counts. Merely addressing the general topic or the view overall without pointing to specific OP text does not count. Return 0 if the list is valid and nonempty and no comment does so, provided title/argument are available. Return null if OC_comments is missing/malformed or empty-of-parse, or if OP title/argument is missing so absence cannot be established (a clear positive quote may still yield 1). Do not use the conversation column or later replies. Output 0/1/null.

left_feature.name: counterargument_cognitive_complexity
left_feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments, by users other than OP): overall cognitive complexity of the counterarguments, scored 0-10 by anchored rubric
left_feature.spec: Read the OC_comments JSON list (counter-argument comments by users other than the OP; list order carries no rank or chronology). Judge the cognitive complexity of the counterarguments taken together, using only the comment text (ignore quoted text from others unless adopted by the commenter). Cognitive complexity = differentiation (distinguishing multiple dimensions, perspectives, conditions or cases) plus integration (connecting/weighing them into a nuanced, qualified, reasoned whole), as opposed to simplistic, single-dimension, assertion-only reasoning. Return one number 0-10: 0 = no argumentative content; 2 = bare assertion or single simple point with no reasoning; 4 = one reasoned point with limited elaboration; 6 = several distinct reasons or some acknowledgment of qualifications/alternative views; 8 = multiple dimensions explicitly differentiated with conditions/trade-offs and partly integrated; 10 = highly differentiated and fully integrated, nuanced, multi-perspective reasoning. This is an operational score, not a validated instrument. Do not use length alone. Return null if OC_comments is missing, malformed, or an empty list.

right_feature.spec: Read title, argument (OP view) and OC_comments (JSON list of comments by other users; order is not rank or chronology) jointly. Return 1 if at least one comment directly challenges the OP's stated view with a well-reasoned counterargument: clear, relevant, logically coherent reasoning or evidence that bears on the OP's actual claim, not mere assertion, insult, joke, off-topic remark or pure agreement. left_feature.name: any_comment_quotes_op_text
left_feature.definition: Counter-argument comments (OC_comments, not OP): any comment directly quotes verbatim text from the OP's title or post body
left_feature.spec: Read OC_comments (JSON list of comments by users other than OP), jointly with the OP title and argument (current text, including marked edits). Return 1 if at least one comment contains a direct textual quotation (e.g., quoted or blockquote-marked '>' text, verbatim or near-verbatim excerpt presented as quoting) that matches text in the OP title or argument. Return 0 if the comments are assessable and no such quotation exists. A valid empty list gives 0. Output 1/0/null.

right_feature.name: op_logical_concession_count

right_feature.spec: Read conversation together with title and argument.
